title: Hindsight Is 2024
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he was nursing grudges and claiming a mandate. T...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he was nursing grudges and claiming a mandate. The institutions he saw as his enemies—in politics, business, and education—faced a dilemma about how to respond.

A few concluded that they should resist the president’s demands of fealty and collaboration. Another group tried appeasement, seeking accommodation that would allow them to otherwise operate as usual. And some looked at the landscape and concluded that something fundamental had shifted in American politics. They saw the MAGA movement as a lasting change, and decided that their best move was to make their own radical shift to adjust.

As I wrote last week, predictions of a Trump-driven realignment of the electorate now look extremely shaky. The groups that he was able to attract to the Republican ticket two years ago—young voters, especially men; Hispanic voters; and Black men—have turned solidly against him and against GOP candidates in polls ahead of the midterms. Voters who were unimpressed with Joe Biden or Kamala Harris and who heard Trump’s promise of stopping inflation are now angry about the president’s shrugging at higher prices and inflationary war in Iran. With some distance, the 2024 election looks less like a decisive turning point and more like a fluke. But that realization has come too late for those who reshaped themselves for a reality that has proved ephemeral.

David Ellison, who, along with his father, Larry, is a friend of Trump’s, decided to use the new Trump administration as an opportunity to build a huge media conglomerate. First, his company Skydance merged with Paramount. Taking control of CBS News, he installed Bari Weiss as editor in chief, seeking a leader who would appeal more to both the White House and to conservative viewers. But Weiss’s makeover has so far looked like a flop: 60 Minutes has hemorrhaged staffers, and the Evening News has hemorrhaged viewers. Her proposition was that a slightly more conservative version of the mainstream media would bring the audience back to a struggling network, but that doesn’t appear to actually be appealing to either MAGA viewers or legacy CBS watchers.

Ellison has already moved on to an attempted merger with Warner Bros., reportedly promising administration officials deep political changes at CNN if the deal was approved by federal regulators. Ellison got approval, but now that deal is in trouble anyway. Facing an antitrust lawsuit led by the attorney general of California, Paramount agreed to pause the merger until a trial next year. Experts are divided on how likely Paramount is to prevail, but if the merger doesn’t close by September 30, the company will owe Warner Bros. shareholders $7 million every day until it does. In a New York Times column last week, Ellison complained that people are drawing incorrect inferences about his politics, but his private views are beside the point: What is public is Ellison’s willingness to play to the Trump administration’s politics to build an empire.

CBS News is not the only media interest to discover that courting MAGA news consumers is not a guarantee of success or growth. The Times also reported recently on how a range of right-wing influencers has seen audiences shrink drastically. Their travails appear to reflect Trump’s own difficulty in keeping his 2024 coalition together: The most pro-Trump figures have seen some of the biggest drops, amid ideological battles inside the MAGA coalition over Israel and the war in Iran, while more Trump-critical figures on the right have sometimes gained.

Other corporate leaders also bet on Trump. Elon Musk attempted to become something like an unelected deputy president at the start of Trump’s second term. That experiment ended acrimoniously, and the men’s relationship has been on and off ever since, but Musk’s reputation is now inextricably connected with Trump’s. X has shed users. Tesla sales have struggled, in part because anti-Trump consumers have turned against Musk and also because Musk has been distracted by other ventures, such as SpaceX.

These decisions to throw in with Trump were notable because many institutions treated his 2016 win as an accident of chance, and were happy to publicly resist him. In doing so, though, they seem to have opened the door to more direct corporate involvement in politics—and with it, greater vulnerability to political pressure. The idea that corporations had gone “woke” by embracing DEI and other progressive causes in 2020 and 2021 was to some extent a marketing ploy by the companies, but it infuriated Republicans and made them targets for Trump’s second administration. Trying to protect themselves, corporate leaders now may have overcorrected, mistakenly assuming a lasting MAGA regime.

Within right-wing politics, many individuals and organizations also leapt into Trumpism. The venerable Heritage Foundation reworked itself and lost or pushed out many long-standing scholars and staffers. Now it finds itself in an identity crisis—and also shut out of the White House because Trump is still sore about the attention and credit that Project 2025 won for driving his agenda. Many mainstream Republicans remade themselves as MAGA Republicans, but the results have not always been good. Just ask Senator John Cornyn, who lost his primary to an even-more-MAGA challenger this May.

Earlier this month, Politico’s Kathy Gilsinan reported on the broken pipeline for bringing new foot soldiers into conservative government and nonprofit organizations. “Everyone knows what the problem is: The organizations that bring young staffers to Washington, D.C. have spent the last decade prioritizing blind ideological loyalty instead of competence or intelligence,” a senior GOP congressional staffer told her. “We have a generation of rabid, incompetent idiots.”

This is the risk of betting big on a long-term realignment: If you wager wrong, politics overall will snap back quickly, but you will be stuck with the consequences of your decision for much longer.

Today’s News

  1. A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 111 people and causing building collapses, injuries, and widespread damage, according to Colombian officials.
  2. President Trump told Axios that the United States is only “semi-negotiating” with Iran as talks over reopening the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled after Tehran laid out its demands, including compensation for war damage.
  3. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the Trump administration’s 15-point Gaza plan yesterday, saying that Israel will not withdraw its forces until Hamas is fully disarmed. The proposal, announced by Trump’s Board of Peace last month, called for Hamas to surrender its weapons in phases in exchange for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.

Illustration by Lucy Murray Willis / The Atlantic

If Only This Could Last Forever

By Elizabeth Bruenig

Summer always overstays its welcome by about a month. After the Fourth of July, which has its charms, nothing but a stretch of relentless heat lies ahead, reaching toward Labor Day, and I begin to yearn for fall. So does the grand, semi-malevolent intelligence that organizes American consumption: By mid-August, grocery stores are stocking their shelves with autumnal goods—pumpkin-pie Pop-Tarts, cinnamon-maple Frosted Flakes, pumpkin-spice cinnamon rolls in pressurized cardboard tubes. As I stroll through the aisles, I gaze wistfully at candy corn while the frosty supermarket air cools the sweat I worked up walking to the store beneath the blazing sun. Late September can’t arrive soon enough.

title: Photos: European Rivers Fall to Record Lows
summary:

Fadel Dawod / GettyA marina is seen surrounded by exposed riverbed as water levels remain low along the Waal River in Nijmegen, Netherland...
content:
Michael Probst / AP
The Pfalzgrafenstein toll castle sits in the middle of the Rhine River, seen at a very low water level, in Kaub, Germany, on August 10, 2026.
Fadel Dawod / Getty
A marina is seen surrounded by exposed riverbed as water levels remain low along the Waal River in Nijmegen, Netherlands, on August 8, 2026. The Netherlands is facing an ongoing drought and water shortage as exceptionally low river flows continue across the country. The low water levels are affecting inland shipping—vessels are forced to reduce their loads as navigable depths decrease.
Djordje Kojadinovic / Reuters
A drone view shows people swimming near a sunken German warship from World War II, exposed due to low water levels in the Danube River, in Prahovo, Serbia, on July 30, 2026.
Nenad Mihajlovic / AFP / Getty
People walk across sandbars exposed by the low water level of the Danube River near Apatin, Serbia, on August 4, 2026.
Fabrice Coffrini / AFP / Getty
This aerial photograph shows the parched bed of Brenets Lake (Lac des Brenets), part of the Doubs River, a natural border between eastern France and western Switzerland, on July 28, 2026. The river has dried up due to a combination of factors, including geological fissures that drain water underground, below-average rainfall, and repeated heat waves.
Oliver Berg / DPA / Getty
An inland waterway vessel sails past the cathedral on the Rhine in Cologne, Germany, at low water levels, on July 31, 2026.
Marton Monus / Reuters
A drone view of a cruise ship that became stranded due to the low water level of the Danube River near Gönyű, Hungary, on August 1, 2026.
Mike Kemp / In Pictures / Getty
A water-level marker sits above the low water on the River Redlake in Bucknell, England, on July 24, 2026.
Andrej Isakovic / AFP / Getty
This aerial photo shows boats in a marina left stranded on the riverbed by the low water level of the Danube River in Novi Sad, Serbia, on August 7, 2026.
Akos Stiller / Bloomberg / Getty
Visitors gather on an exposed section of riverbed on the Danube River during a heat wave in Budapest, Hungary, on August 8, 2026.
Remo Casilli / Reuters
A drone view shows the Po River running low under Gerola Bridge as drought conditions threaten nearby rice fields, in Mezzana Bigli, Italy, on August 6, 2026
Andreea Alexandru / AP
A man splashes water on a horse to cool it off next to a riverbank of the Danube River, as usually submerged areas are exposed due to extreme low water levels in Roseti, Romania, on July 29, 2026.
Christian Bruna / Getty
People walk along the exposed lake bottom of the severely shrunk Nussensee mountain lake during ongoing drought and hot weather on August 2, 2026, near Bad Ischl, Austria.
Dominika Zarzycka / SOPA Images / LightRocket / Getty
People walk on an unusually wide beach on the south bank of Thames River in central London on August 7, 2026.
Robert Nemeti / Anadolu / Getty
A cyclist rides along the dry riverbed of the Danube near the Paks Nuclear Power Plant on August 9, 2026. The plant is currently operating with only one of its four reactors at minimum output, an unprecedented situation in its nearly 40-year history, as historically low Danube water levels have constrained the plant’s cooling capacity.
Robert Nemeti / Anadolu via Getty / Anadolu
A person explores the exposed riverbed of the Danube, after low water levels revealed the remains of an old World War II–era ship from the riverbed in Baja, Hungary, on August 8, 2026.
Andrej Isakovic / AFP / Getty
This photo shows a dried-out sunflower field near the village of Kovilj, Serbia, near the Danube River, on August 6, 2026, during a prolonged heat wave.
Boris Roessler / DPA / Getty
Extremely low water levels on the Rhine expose the riverbed near Bacharach, Germany, behind Stahleck Castle, on August 10, 2026.

title: Never Trump, Still a Republican
summary: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket CastsJeff Flake is something of a maverick in today’s Republican Party. He was an early and consistent critic of President Trump. In December 2015, when then-candidate Trump floated a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims enter...
content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Jeff Flake is something of a maverick in today’s Republican Party. He was an early and consistent critic of President Trump. In December 2015, when then-candidate Trump floated a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering” the United States—a preview of what became his now-infamous executive order barring travel to the U.S. by people from several Muslim-majority countries—Flake, then a United States senator from Arizona, immediately spoke up. The idea repulsed him. He made a visit to a mosque in Scottsdale days later to declare that what people were seeing from Trump on the campaign trail was not representative of America.

“This was a difficult week in Washington—it wasn’t so much the legislative calendar as it was the rhetoric that came forth mostly from the presidential campaign,” Flake, who is a practicing Mormon, said. It was his first visit to a mosque. “That is not in keeping with the values and ideals that have made this country the shining city on the hill that it is.”

Trump went on to win that election. And Flake could no longer stomach the direction his party was headed. He would have been up for reelection in 2018 but decided against running again. As he told my colleague McKay Coppins at the time, he was not interested in the kind of campaign he’d had to have run to win—or even simply to secure Trump’s endorsement. In a memorable speech, Flake decried the deterioration of politics and called for America to look toward its better angels.

It’s been almost a decade since that speech and Trump’s hold over the Republican Party shows few signs of weakening any time soon. Meanwhile, Flake recently endorsed Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator from Georgia, in Ossoff’s reelection bid over the Trump-endorsed Representative Mike Collins. What does it mean to be a Republican when the party has moved away from the things it has historically claimed to stand for? On this week’s Radio Atlantic, Flake joins me to discuss his endorsement, the Senate, and the party he hopes to reclaim.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Adam Harris: What does it mean to continue identifying with the party if it’s moved beyond the recognition of what it’s been in the past? Which is sort of to say, are you hanging on to a party that isn’t your party anymore?

Jeff Flake: That would be, you know, easy to say right now, but parties sometimes return as well. You see parties flirt with populism and then return, and I’m hopeful that that’s what you see now.

Harris: I’m Adam Harris. This is Radio Atlantic, and this week, a conversation with former Republican U.S. Senator and Ambassador Jeff Flake. We talk about the state of the Republican Party, the Senate, and what it means to be principled in politics.

Flake is known for crossing party lines. Most recently, he endorsed Georgia’s Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff in his reelection campaign against Mike Collins. Collins, of course, is the Trump-endorsed Republican congressman from Georgia.

In announcing his endorsement, Flake told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution that his decision boiled down to character, saying: “Character is more important. I’ve been around long enough to know you’ll disagree on issues with people across the aisle, or sometimes in your party. But the more important thing is character.”

In 2017, Flake delivered a fiery speech where he announced that he would not run for another term in office.

Flake: “There are times where we must risk our careers in favor of our principles. Now is such a time.”

Harris: He believed the shift in the Republican party was temporary; he believed the fever would break.

But it’s been almost a decade since that speech. Does he still think that’s possible?

Ambassador Flake joins me now to discuss. Let’s get to questions.

Ambassador, thank you for joining me.

Flake: Hey, thanks for having me on.

Harris: What to you are the characteristics of a moral candidate, of a candidate with character?

Flake: Well, I want somebody who respects the institution of the Senate. And, you know, the Senate and senators have always very jealously guarded their prerogative to push back against any president from their own party or not. That’s just kind of been a hallmark of the Senate. You have six-year terms; you’re more independent; you have more rules than the House does in terms of advise and consent.

Then, too, I would fit in character as well. I have a hard time with people who simply won’t admit the obvious—one when your president loses an election and you’re afraid to tell him. That, I think, doesn’t speak well for character.

So yeah, in this case we have that problem as well. Senator Ossoff’s opponent, you know, simply won’t admit, and claims that President Trump won in Georgia and won the 2020 election. That doesn’t speak well for character. Also with character, it’s realizing in the Senate, too, with the special rules, the supermajority rules of filibuster, that you’re a legislator; you work across the aisle. And I’ve seen Senator Ossoff do that on a number of occasions sponsoring legislation. And then, constituent service as well. When I was ambassador in Turkey, I got calls from Jon Ossoff. I got to know him then because he was advocating on behalf of some of his constituents. So anyway, I’ve been impressed with him.

Harris: I have to reference the speech from the Senate floor in 2017, because it was such a succinct articulation of democratic values and principles. You argued in that speech that “anger and resentment is not a governing strategy,” and you took particular issue with your party’s acquiescence in that regard. How has that dynamic changed at all in the years since, for better or worse?

Flake: Unfortunately, it hasn’t gotten better in terms of my party and, you know, our willingness to stand up and actually govern. As I mentioned before, anger and grievance are not a governing philosophy, but we’ve just kind of fallen in and decided that whatever the president wants, whatever the party wants, that’s where we are. And that unfortunately has not changed much.

You see some people standing up when they’re not running for reelection anymore or have been defeated in a primary, but we need to stand up more. That’s why I like divided government.  You know, a fiscal conservative, I Iook back over the past few decades and the only time we’ve really had good fiscal discipline is when we’ve had divided government. Republicans in particular act more responsible and act more as fiscal conservatives when sometimes we’re in the minority.

Harris: Do you think there will be consequences for the fact that things haven’t gotten better? Do you think that there will be a migration away from the GOP?

Flake: I do, I do. You know, Donald Trump has led a charmed existence politically and he seems to be given a pass that others aren’t given. And if you look around, his imitators have not done well. In Georgia, they haven’t, and in Arizona, where I come from. Arizona is a very red state. We have more than 300,000, you know, more Republicans registered than Democrats.

But we have a Democrat in the governor’s office, two Democratic senators, Democrat secretary of state, and Democrat attorney general—all the elected statewide offices—because we’ve had people try to imitate the president and haven’t done well.

I do think that we’re gonna see a migration, and I’ve written about this, away from the president and his policies. And one, the president has been able to basically control any primary, Republican primary, across the country. That’s waning. And if a president leaves office or is in the last two years of his term, if his policies are really popular, that still lends him power that he wouldn’t otherwise have as a lame duck. But the president’s policies have not done well, in particular, you know, tariff policies, protectionist policies, have led to high inflation, and then also couple that with a war that’s been not popular at all and so, yeah, I think you’re seeing a migration now that, you know—filing deadlines have passed, most primaries have passed, and we’re into the midterm general. And then beyond the midterms, you’ll really see that happening.

Harris: I should ask, do you still identify as a Republican?

Flake: I do, I do. I’m still a registered Republican, and I’m hoping that the party returns to its previous kind of tenets of limited government, economic freedom, individual responsibility, strong American leadership abroad. And I do think that we’re gonna see a return to that. And I think you saw in the Senate, for example, the other day a vote on Russian sanctions. That is a bit of a proxy vote, support for Ukraine but also a support for American leadership, and support for NATO, and support for kind of the old bicameral consensus on foreign policy. So I think you see in elected officials a desire to go back to that, but it’s been very difficult when the president has had such a hold on the party base.

Harris: What does it mean to continue identifying with the party if it’s moved beyond the recognition of what it’s been in the past? Which is sort of to say, are you hanging on to a party that isn’t your party anymore?

Flake: Well that would be easy to say right now, but like I say, parties sometimes return as well. You see parties flirt with populism and then return.

We’re in unfamiliar territory right now, and I think we’re going to be migrating back to more familiar ground. And I do think that that’s where the country really is. I think we’re a center-right country. But the problem right now is, you know, you only have a subset of a subset of a subset that votes in Republican primaries. You have a similar issue on the Democratic side, not as pronounced perhaps, but that just puts all the political incentives to drive to the extremes. But I don’t think that’s where the country is.

That’s why one thing that really excites me about people like Jon Ossoff is I think that they can move the Democratic Party more to its, more to the center, and that would force Republicans to then contest that ground as well. As long as we have Democrats, you know, all the energy on the far progressive side, it allows Republicans to be extreme as well and still be seen as less extreme, I guess.

Harris: Well, actually, I wanted to stick with that for a second, because you’ve said there’s this sort of massive lane in the middle, that most people identify as politically in the middle, but Democratic voters in recent primaries have shown that that’s not exactly where they are either, right? There’s been this feeling that things are broken in part because of some of the middle-ground solutions, right? They’re part of what has led us to this moment where you see candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan winning the Democratic primary. So, I guess, what does success from the left wing of the Democratic Party tell us about what Americans actually might want right now?

Flake: Yeah, well I think it just proves the point I made before, that when you’re looking at primaries, although there was increased turnout, certainly in Michigan, it’s still a subset of a subset that are determining who the nominee is. And I do think the Democrats in Michigan would have been far better off by, you know, going a different direction. I think they would have had that general election easily. Now it’ll be more difficult, certainly. But I do think, yeah, the same problem is on both sides. I think without a polarizing figure like Donald Trump, who certainly controls primaries on the right and causes Democrats to act in ways that they wouldn’t otherwise. I see people like Gavin Newsom using foul and crude language just because the president does and he wants to match it. And you see that phenomenon all over, and it’s not not been good for politics. I hope we can move away from it. But that’s gonna require leadership. That’s why, in particular I appreciate Jon Ossoff, who’s more of a serious candidate and doesn’t kind of follow that.

Harris: Thinking about that speech from 2017, and where we’ve come since then, right, it’s been roughly a decade. All three branches of government right now have really abysmal approval ratings. People’s trust in institutions is flagging, and you said that the spell will eventually break, right? Once there’s no longer a Trump, we can return to ourselves once more. It seems that you’re still of that belief that the fever is going to break. What are you seeing that gives you that hope that the fever’s going to break?

Flake: Well, it’s been one heck of a fever. It’s been a long time in coming. Well, one, let me just say, I was back in Washington for Lindsey Graham’s funeral last week, and I came away from that believing that, like I’ve said, that this fever will break.

One, I saw Democrats and Republicans. Lindsey was an interesting figure, but if nothing else, he certainly had friends on the Democratic side. I was with him on a lot of those issues on immigration reform in particular and a lot of the foreign-policy issues. And you saw people from all political stripes come out and celebrate a man’s life that way. That made me feel good. At the same time, you had Senators [John] Cornyn and [Thom] Tillis standing up—albeit they’re not staying in Washington after January—but hey, it’s still something to actually stand up to the president and see the Senate acting more like the Senate again.

And I see John Thune keeping some of his members at bay who want to make institutional changes, like getting rid of the filibuster, which would fundamentally change the Senate into a more partisan body than it already is. But I came away from this week even more firmly believing that, you know, this fever will break. And when you look around the country as well, I still think you see that phenomenon that the president’s imitators don’t do as well as he does. So I’m hopeful that that fever will break.

Harris: But you’ve written, right, that we’ve seen folks in the past, lawmakers, the country generally, come together after death or after a tragedy? Two of which you experienced at the congressional baseball practice as well as standing with Representative [Gabby] Giffords at the State of the Union.

But that quickly fades away, and people sort of divide again. Do you think that even if we do heal that there will be that division again?

Flake: Yeah, well, I think you’ve had a lot of people elected, particularly in the last several cycles, who haven’t really been in Washington when there’s been so-called regular order, or, you know, what we’re used to. So it’s gonna be difficult. You’ll always have those voices, and we have a media environment that’s not going back to the way it was before, where there are just a few trusted sources of information. It’s more distributed that way. So it’s more difficult to go back to the way it was. But that’s why it’s going to require real leadership. And leadership is important. We’ve seen that, because the man in the White House now, he’s certainly been effective in where he’s wanted to go and getting people on his side more out of fear of losing primaries. But, by the same token, you’re going to have leaders that actually inspire people, better angels of our nature, and that’s what I’m hoping to see in this next presidential election is people on both the Republican and the Democratic side who will appeal to people’s better angels. And if they do, I think we can get to a better place. It’s gonna be more difficult moving ahead, like I said, just because of the media environment, but it’s not impossible.

Harris: Well, ambassador, we’ll have to leave it there. It’s been a pleasure. Thank you so much for joining me today.

Flake: Thanks for having me on.

title: If Only This Could Last Forever
summary: Summer always overstays its welcome by about a month. After the Fourth of July, which has its charms, nothing but a stretch of relentless heat lies ahead, reaching toward Labor Day, and I begin to yearn for fall. So does the grand, semi-malevolent intelligence that organizes American consumption: By...
content:
Summer always overstays its welcome by about a month. After the Fourth of July, which has its charms, nothing but a stretch of relentless heat lies ahead, reaching toward Labor Day, and I begin to yearn for fall. So does the grand, semi-malevolent intelligence that organizes American consumption: By mid-August, grocery stores are stocking their shelves with autumnal goods—pumpkin-pie Pop-Tarts, cinnamon-maple Frosted Flakes, pumpkin-spice cinnamon rolls in pressurized cardboard tubes. As I stroll through the aisles, I gaze wistfully at candy corn while the frosty supermarket air cools the sweat I worked up walking to the store beneath the blazing sun. Late September can’t arrive soon enough.

This summer has been especially hot, worse than most years. Heat waves killed at least 14,000 people in Europe; parts of France recorded 110-degree temperatures in June. Wildfires raged across North America, torching more than 4.5 million acres in Canada and parts of the United States, and forcing 60,000 people to evacuate their homes. The Canadian fires sent heavy smoke billowing over the Northeast, coloring the sky, contaminating the air, and forcing all activities indoors. The warming climate has brought too many ticks and a 10 to 15 percent rise in mosquitoes, along with raised red welts and transmitted viruses. All of this was on my mind as I slathered my children with insect repellent and sunscreen before sending them off to local playgrounds half-consumed by green overgrowth, poison ivy lurking among the leaves. Still, no amount of well-intended prophylaxis stands a chance against little hands and streams of sweat.

[Sarah Zhang: Kill the ticks]

The season comes with a chaotic flurry of activity as the last school bell gives way to day camps, sleepaway camps, and hastily cobbled-together child care spread out, with luck, among family and friends—unwieldy arrangements that cost the average parent thousands of dollars a year. My two daughters arrive home from day camp hours before the workday is done, with dirt on their knees and Popsicle sticks between their teeth. I scramble to squeeze in snacks and entertainment between sentences: peanut-butter-and-jelly crackers here, a paint-by-number kit there, both kids as bored as I am busy. The front yard is apparently too flat to supply sufficient fun on the Slip ’N Slide, though my daughters still scoot valiantly on it when the afternoon grows too monotonous. I hose the grass off their feet and lay down towels before they come back inside, then stay up late doing dishes and laundry after they go to bed.

Another item of business: Both children have summer birthdays, and the pressure of whipping up summertime birthday parties can be enormous. Convening dozens of children during vacation season takes some wrangling. This year, I packed 26 piping bags of icing in a rainbow of pastel colors and made tiny cakes for one daughter and her friends to decorate while seated at long folding tables on the back patio. I also lugged a helium tank and bags of banners, tablecloths, hats, and balloons to the ice-skating rink, and nervously prayed that enough kids would show up to satisfy my other daughter. It all transpired smoothly in the end, and then I found myself with cake crumbs on my shorts and a 10-year-old and 7-year-old, wondering where the time had gone. Summer drags on but then feels fleeting. It’s hard not to experience a certain nostalgia for the moments as they pass.

Still, one works up a sweat managing the hours, such that it comes as something of a relief when the kids abscond to sleepaway camp for a couple of weeks, or to the beach with Grandma and Grandpa for a little while. The house is clean and quiet, and the work gets done. I comb through their old clothes, folding the old ones into donation bags to make room for back-to-school outfits that are one or two sizes larger than last year’s.

[Russell Shaw: The new parent trap]

But there are still a few weeks of summer left when they come home, and though there are dishes in the sink, mud tracks on the floor, and deadlines to meet, I join them on their adventures. We sail across the New York Harbor by ferry to Governors Island, a kids’ oasis where the fresh waters of the Hudson River stream into the salty Atlantic Ocean. There are food trucks, ice-cream stands, enormous slides, and a massive junkyard playground where kids can splatter paint across scrap wood and mount precariously assembled tire forts. It is hot—searing hot—but what I see when I squint through the sweat is resplendent, kids climbing the structures of their own worlds. My two daughters are golden-skinned, with sun-bleached braids; their fine, downy body hair catches the light, lending them an ethereal glow. They look like young gods in the summertime of their lives. This season is their season. The junkyard play feels a little dangerous, but it’s their beauty, not their vulnerability, that transfixes me. When night comes, I help them ignite leftover sparklers, which illuminate their faces with silvery starlight.

Fall arrives like a fever breaking. Mayhem gives way to order, and adventures give way to routines. A cool calmness presides over suburbia. And as I heave heavy pumpkins into my cart at Costco, I know that I will soon get what I have eagerly anticipated: darkness and quiet, discipline and fruitful maturity. I will clock out of work for the day just as the children arrive home from school, hang their backpacks by the door, and huddle around the kitchen table. They will have spent their day learning new skills and new social norms, developing their friendships and knowledge of the world. All of this will change them, subtly but certainly. At these ages, they are constantly being reborn. They still need me to help them with their homework, and they still need me to serve them dinner as the evening proceeds. But they will need me less than they did last year, and next year even less. And as I watch them diligently spell out answers on their worksheets, I will wish that summer had lasted forever.

title: In Defense of Flock
summary: Crime in San Francisco, Jarico Anderson announced last year, “is over with.” Anderson, who raps under the stage name Dreamllife Rizzy, would know—he’s a convicted felon. content:
Crime in San Francisco, Jarico Anderson announced last year, “is over with.” Anderson, who raps under the stage name Dreamllife Rizzy, would know—he’s a convicted felon. Lately, though, he says that cameras have been making criminal life inconvenient. “Soon as you slide past that motherfucker with some stolen plates, they going to issue a warning to every SFPD station in that area, if not the entire city, and they going to start dispatching” officers to that area, Anderson said on an episode of the popular hip-hop and culture podcast No Jumper. “And when they catch you, they’re going to catch you.”

The “motherfucker” in question is an automatic license-plate reader (ALPR)—a camera installed on a light pole or a building that photographs and identifies license plates as they pass below, then adds the image to a centralized database. San Francisco’s roughly 500 ALPRs are provided by Flock Safety, a police-technology firm that claims its ALPRs are deployed in the jurisdictions of more than 5,000 agencies nationwide, recording billions of plate images a month. Networked together, Flock cameras can enable police to track cars in real time, giving them eyes across a city. The cameras also create a record of where cars have been, providing a view of millions of drivers’ movements.

Criminals aren’t the only ones upset about the system. Privacy and civil-rights groups call ALPRs an Orwellian threat to the Fourth Amendment. In cities such as Oakland, California; St. Petersburg, Florida; and Pocatello, Idaho, people have started vandalizing or blocking the cameras. Recently, Flock has become a fixation of the populist right. Last month, Tucker Carlson released an hour-long video claiming that Flock represents the “largest mass-surveillance operation in history” as part of “the coming slave state.” The populist firebrand Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky wants to withhold federal funds from cities that use Flock cameras; Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida wants to ban them outright.

That’s an overreaction. Although research on Flock’s effectiveness is still in the making, ALPRs are likely a valuable tool for any modern police force. Privacy concerns can be best addressed through smart regulation, not bans. Indeed, in our surveillance-saturated society, police cameras can help make the criminal-justice system both fairer and less punitive—if we let them.

[Adam Serwer: Trump should need a warrant to see your phone]

The case for Flock is simple. Cameras help police catch criminals. That reduces crime through two channels: incapacitating offenders who are caught and convicted, and increasing the certainty of apprehension, which theoretically should deter criminals from offending in the first place. But is it true in practice? Although the research base is still developing, the answer is “probably.”

An initial wave of randomized controlled trials from the early 2010s generally found little or no crime-reducing benefit of ALPRs, except a possible reduction in drug-related crime. But these studies collected small samples from small areas and relied on now-decades-old technology. A handful of more recent papers gave reason for optimism, but use weaker research designs that do less to isolate causality. A 2017 study found ALPRs were correlated with a reduction in violent crime; a 2019 paper found suggestive but not conclusive evidence of a reduction in auto theft and robbery; and a 2025 evaluation of Atlantic City’s ALPRs found a reduction in shootings, car thefts, and property crimes. But none of these papers could prove that ALPRs caused these improvements.

There are, however, studies that look at so-called natural experiments—where chance makes an intervention random enough to study it like a randomized trial—that show that cameras in general reduce crime. An analysis exploiting the quasi-random distribution of cameras in Medellin, Colombia, found that they reduced crime by about 19 percent. Another paper showed a 25 percent reduction in crime in subway stations in Stockholm, Sweden, after cameras were installed in them. A third found a 20 percent reduction in areas of Montevideo, Uruguay, where cameras were introduced. And a fourth estimates that nearly tripling cameras per capita in China reduced crime by about 10 percent. ALPRs aren’t exactly the same thing as surveillance cameras, but the consistent effect of the latter on crime should give people more confidence that the former can reduce it, especially in combination with the newer ALPR literature.

Still, many will blanch at using evidence from China to support putting more cameras in American cities. Even if ALPRs make us safer, we are trading at least a little privacy for that security. There are legitimate concerns, too, regarding police abuse of the technology. The Institute for Justice, a libertarian public-interest law firm, has counted 30 cases where officers have used Flock cameras to “stalk romantic interests.” And surveillance critics have warned that ICE has used Flock data in its immigration crackdown.

These are legitimate concerns, and the privacy threat here is real—but, compared with other intrusions, minimal. In principle, ALPRs collect information about cars’ license plates—a government-issued registration that is required for driving on publicly funded roads. The Supreme Court has been quite clear that “a person traveling in an automobile on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in his movements.” Additionally, Americans have, through the cameras nearly everyone carries in their pockets, voluntarily made far more invasive surveillance a regular feature of daily life. Many people may not like that, but it’s hard to see ALPRs as a major intrusion by comparison.

Although a single photo of a moving car is not a major intrusion, a database full of billions of such photos might be. Such “mosaic” surveillance—so named because many small police actions can add up over time to what counts as a “search” in constitutional law—has faced increasing scrutiny from the Supreme Court over the past decade. A single ALPR photo isn’t a search for purposes of the Fourth Amendment’s prohibition on “unreasonable search and seizure,” but the Court has recently found queries of similarly detailed data sets to be a search that requires a court-issued warrant to conduct. (Most queries to a department’s ALPR database currently do not require such a warrant.)

The theory of “mosaic” searches is still evolving, and it’s not obvious whether Flock’s system meets the emerging standard for a search. Still, the general concern is sound—most people would consider a police department keeping unlimited, detailed information on everyone’s movements highly intrusive.

Concerns about such systematic surveillance aren’t trivial, especially when that surveillance is done by the government. The Fourth Amendment’s protections exist exactly because of the very real potential for abuse of police officers’ extraordinary powers. The question, though, is whether we need to forgo the crime-reducing benefits of ALPRs in order to minimize the risks to our privacy. Such absolutism is unwarranted: Smart regulations can help obviate these concerns without getting rid of ALPRs entirely.

One easy step would be to set limits on how long departments can retain ALPR data, something several states have already done. (Flock defaults to a 30-day retention period, which some states have lowered by statute to 21—reasonable windows of time for catching criminals while avoiding creating a permanent record of everyone else’s movements.)

States and police departments can also impose stricter rules about access to ALPR data, including requiring supervisory approval and mandating a log of all access to the database to deter abuse and make it easier to identify. Actual ICE queries are a tiny fraction of total searches, but if a city or state doesn’t want ICE accessing their database, they can make that rule easily. Both states and departments can also increase penalties for abusing an ALPR system—there’s no reason to treat cops as immune if they engage in such wrongdoing.

[Read: How license-plate readers have helped police and lenders target the poor]

When critics fixate on abuses, they miss the way that cameras can make policing and punishment more humane. Many approaches to reducing crime rely on increasing the severity of punishment—ratcheting up prison sentences or expanding mass incarceration. The promise of high-tech policing, using cameras and DNA databases, is that it can deter crime without such extreme measures, and as a result demand less overall punishment from the system as a whole.

Take Anderson’s car-thief associates. If they know that a camera will help catch them, they become less likely to steal. If they don’t offend, they aren’t caught, arrested, and incarcerated. Consequently, both crime and punishment fall, leaving everyone better off.

The benefits of that arrangement accrue, in a sense, to criminals. But they accrue far more to the law-abiding. Crime imposes an enormous cost on society—trillions of dollars in time, money, suffering, and lives lost. Criminal victimization can scar people for years after, a fact that shows up in everything from how much they work to how dependent they are on government benefits. Assuming we take reasonable precautions to protect our liberty and privacy, having ALPRs help reduce these costs is clearly worth it.

Flock cameras are an easy target for a populist backlash. But although some of the concerns are reasonable, a panic about a “slave state” shouldn’t determine public policy. Intelligently regulated, ALPRs can be one among many tools in the toolbox of smarter—and therefore less severe—police forces. Dumping the cameras would just be foolish.

title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
summary: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to CeutaSpain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.The checks, which come “am...
content:
Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta

Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

content:
Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians

Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

content:
Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation

The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
summary: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and CameroonThe US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of bei...
content:
State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon

The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone

The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.
